Highlights 3

• STAMP identifies binding sites of full-length RBPs by C-to-U RNA editing. 4

• STAMP coupled to long read sequencing reveals isoform specific RBP targets. 5

Abstract 0

1

2

RNA binding proteins (RBPs) are critical regulators of gene expression and RNA processing that are 3

required for gene function. Yet, the dynamics of RBP regulation in single cells is unknown. To address this gap 4

in understanding, we developed STAMP (Surveying Targets by APOBEC Mediated Profiling), which efficiently 5

detects RBP-RNA interactions. STAMP does not rely on UV-crosslinking or immunoprecipitation and, when 6

coupled with single-cell capture, can identify RBP- and cell type-specific RNA-protein interactions for multiple 7

RBPs and cell types in single-pooled experiments. Pairing STAMP with long-read sequencing also yields RBP 8

target sites for full-length isoforms. Finally, conducting STAMP using small ribosomal subunits (Ribo-STAMP) 9

allows analysis of transcriptome-wide ribosome association in single cells. STAMP enables the study of RBP- 0

RNA interactomes and translational landscapes with unprecedented cellular resolution. 1

Introduction 8

9

RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) interact with RNA molecules from synthesis to decay to affect their 0

metabolism, localization, stability and translation [1, 2]. Methods for transcriptome-wide detection of RBP-RNA 1

interactions provide insights into how RBPs control gene expression programs and how RNA processing is 2

disrupted in disease states [3, 4]. Immunoprecipitation-based technologies coupled to high throughput 3

sequencing such as RNA Immunoprecipitation (RIP) and Crosslinking Immunoprecipitation (CLIP) are commonly 4

used to identify RBP targets and binding sites across the transcriptome [5]. The eukaryotic ribosome is itself 5

composed of a collection of RBPs that can interact directly with mRNA coding sequences [3, 6]. Ribosome 6

profiling methods such as ribo-seq, like CLIP-seq, have become a mainstay in the evaluation of transcriptome- 7

scale translational efficiency [7, 8]. Unfortunately, CLIP and ribosome profiling experimental protocols are labor- 8

intensive and usually require sizable amounts of input material [9, 10], and are not amenable for experiments 9

that necessitate low input material or single cell resolution, and also are unable to resolve target transcript 0

isoforms due to transcript fragmentation. In contrast, there has been rapid progress in single-cell measurements 1

of chromatin accessibility [11], gene expression [12, 13], and even surface protein-levels [14, 15].  However, 2

there is currently no available technology or documented demonstration that we can measure RBP and ribosome 3

interaction sites on mRNA at single cell level resolution. 4

As a step towards lowering input requirements for RBP-recognition, recent studies have circumvented 5

the need for immunoprecipitation by utilizing fusions of RNA-editing or RNA-modifying modules to RBPs of 6

interest to label RNA targets. This field of antibody-free RBP-RNA interactome detection has grown steadily in 7

recent years. The first demonstration of this general strategy, termed “RNA-tagging”, utilized fusion to 8

the Caenorhabditis elegans poly(U) polymerase PUP-2 to RBPs to covalently mark target 3’ ends with poly(U) 9

chains, which allowed transcriptome-wide target identification in Saccharomyces cerevisiae [16]. This poly(U) 0

tagging was recently extended to probe RNA localization by tethering fusions to the endoplasmic reticulum or to 1

the mitochondria [17].  These poly(U) tagging approaches unfortunately cannot provide information about binding 2

site locations within identified target RNAs and have not been evaluated for low cell input from multicellular 3

systems. Internal RNA target labeling has been recently accomplished by the Target of RNA-binding proteins 4

Identified by Editing (TRIBE) approach, which fuses RBPs of interest to the deaminase domain from the ADAR 5

family of RNA-editing enzymes to mark target RNAs with A-to-I edits [18]. TRIBE allowed detection of RBP 6

targets using as little as 150 Drosophila neurons, and the approach has since been updated using an ADAR 7

hyperactivating mutation to increase editing efficiency (HyperTRIBE) [18-22]. Even with this hyperactivating 8

mutation, these ADAR-mediated approaches are constrained by the sparsity of double-stranded regions 9

proximal to RBP binding sites that are required for ADAR-mediated adenosine to inosine editing [23]. 0

APOBEC1 is a cytosine deaminase that catalyzes RNA cytosine-to-uracil (C-to-U) conversion [24]. 1

Recently APOBEC1 was fused to the m6A-binding YTH domain to identify m6A modification sites on RNAs 2

genome-wide [25]. This approach, termed DART-seq (Deamination Adjacent to RNA modification Target), is 3

distinguished from TRIBE as it departs from using ADAR dsRNA A-to-I editing domains. DART-seq showed 4

precision for identifying m6A-YTH interactions on single stranded mRNAs and demonstrated binding site 5


<!-- Page 4 -->


resolution with good specificity. However, it was unclear if APOBEC1 fusions would work with non-m6A or 6

general classes of RBPs such as splicing factors, RNA stability factors, histone stem-loop binding proteins, or 7

even ribosomes. We reasoned that fusion of APOBEC1 to such full-length RBPs (rather than a section of an 8

RBP such as the YTH domain) could allow for robust, immunoprecipitation-free identification of RBP targets 9

across functional RNA-interaction categories using extremely low or even single-cell input. Here, we demonstrate 0

the utility of such an approach for detecting RBP-RNA targets at the single-cell and single molecule level. We 1

developed an integrated experimental and computational framework termed STAMP (Surveying Targets By 2

APOBEC-Mediated Profiling) which greatly extends the DART-seq approach to demonstrate, for the first time, 3

the discovery of RBP-RNA sites at single-cell resolution, the deconvolution of targets for multiplexed RBPs, and 4

the cell-type specific binding of an RBP in a heterogenous mixtures of cell-types. By applying STAMP with 5

specific ribosome subunits, we also extend this approach for single-cell detection of ribosome association while 6

simultaneously measuring gene expression. Our innovations demonstrate that translation efficiency and RBP- 7

interactomes can be measured at single-cell level, opening up new paradigms for probing biological questions. 8

Results 0

1

STAMP identifies RBP binding sites without immunoprecipitation 2

3

Our strategy for immunoprecipitation-free detection of RBP targets involves fusing an RBP of interest to 4

the cytidine deaminase enzyme APOBEC1, which is known to catalyze C-to-U editing on single-stranded RNA 5

targets (Figure 1A).  We termed this general strategy STAMP (Surveying Targets by APOBEC Mediated 6

Profiling). Upon expression of an RBP-APOBEC1 fusion protein (RBP-STAMP), RBPs direct the deaminase 7

module to specific RNA targets leading to C-to-U base conversion proximal to RBP binding sites.  These 8

mutations are resolved using high-throughput RNA sequencing approaches and quantified using the SAILOR 9

analysis pipeline [26], which we modified to identify and assign a confidence score for C-to-U mismatches using 0

a beta distribution that factors both site coverage and editing percentage (see Materials and Methods) following 1

removal of annotated hg19 SNPs [27]. 2

To determine the utility of the STAMP approach, we fused APOBEC1 to the C-terminus of the RBP 3

RBFOX2 [28-30] and generated stable HEK293T cell lines using lentiviral integration. RBFOX2-STAMP is 4

doxycycline inducible to allow modulation of the duration and magnitude of fusion expression, and we noted no 5

detectable change in cell viability or proliferation rate at any induction level or time point.  Cells expressing low 6

(50ng/ml doxycycline) and high (1µg/ml doxycycline) levels of RBFOX2-STAMP for 72 hours had enriched C-to- 7

U edit clusters on the 3’ untranslated region (3’UTR) of the known RBFOX2 target APP mRNA, and these edit 8

clusters coincided with reproducible RBFOX2 binding sites as detected by enhanced CLIP (eCLIP) [31] (Figure 9

1B). Uninduced RBFOX2-STAMP, or control-STAMP (APOBEC1 only) at low and high induction, had few or no 0

detectible C-to-U edits in the same region, indicating target specificity. RBFOX2-STAMP induced edits within 1

this APP 3’UTR target region were 10-fold to 25-fold more frequent than background control-STAMP edits at 0.9 2


<!-- Page 5 -->


and 0.999 confidence levels, respectively, as called by SAILOR (Figure 1C, Table S1, Table S2). These results 3

demonstrate that fusion of the APOBEC1 module to a well characterized RBP enriches for target-specific edits. 4

To evaluate the reproducibility of STAMP, we conducted replicate control- and RBFOX2-STAMP with low 5

and high doxycycline inductions for 24, 48 and 72 hours.  All RBFOX2-STAMP induction levels and time points 6

showed reproducible edit enrichment on the APP 3’UTR eCLIP peak region (Figure S1A), when compared to 7

undetectable edits from corresponding control-STAMP (Figure S1B). We found that the number of edits 8

(confidence ≥ 0.5) on a given target gene was highly correlated between replicates, and that transcriptome-wide 9

correlations improved with higher RBFOX2-STAMP levels (Figure 1D, Figure S1C).  Irreproducible discovery 0

rate (IDR) analysis [32] revealed hundreds to thousands of reproducible edit clusters for RBFOX2-STAMP, with 1

the number of these reproducible clusters also increasing with levels of RBFOX2-STAMP (Figure S1D).  We 2

also evaluated the effects of RBFOX2-STAMP editing on target transcript levels by conducting differential gene 3

expression analysis on low and high-induction RBFOX2-STAMP at 24, 48 and 72 hours compared to uninduced 4

controls and detected negligible changes in gene expression at these collection points (Figure S1E, Table S3). 5

We next measured the nucleotide distance of RBFOX2-STAMP edits from known RBFOX2 binding sites. 6

For the 2,852 RBFOX2 eCLIP peaks that harbor the canonical RBFOX2 motif GCAUG, distances from the motif 7

to RBFOX2-STAMP and control-STAMP (background) edits were determined within a 400 bp window (Figure 8

1E).  We observed 1,751 edits for RBFOX2-STAMP within 200 bp of binding site motifs inside eCLIP peaks, 9

compared to 97 edits from control-STAMP, indicating that RBFOX2 RNA-binding activity is directing and 0

enriching RBFOX2-specific edits at conserved sites. This RBFOX2-STAMP edit enrichment decreased to 1

background >200 bp away from the motif.  We next measured the number of high confidence (≥ 0.99) edits in 2

100-bp windows centered around RBFOX2 eCLIP peaks within coding sequence (CDS) and 3’UTRs. We saw 3

that ~30% of eCLIP peaks contained at least one high confidence edit, and importantly, the ratio of fractions 4

comparing authentic peaks to randomly located sequences within the same annotated regions (n trials = 100) 5

increased with the number of edits found in each window (blue line in Figure 1F).  To establish a metric for 6

reporting STAMP signal across regions and whole genes that takes into account (i) read coverage over edit site, 7

(ii) edit frequency and (iii) editing potential (C-encoded reference bases), we calculated an edit fraction score (e) 8

as the ratio of the total SAILOR-filtered C-to-U reads over the total SAILOR-filtered mapped reads across every 9

annotated C within a given sequence window. Binning windows evenly across the range of e scores revealed 0

that this score is a strong indicator of edit enrichment (blue line) within eCLIP peaks compared to randomly 1

located regions (Figure 1G). Finally, we performed de novo motif discovery within merged 51-nucleotide 2

windows filtered only by confidence score, assessing enrichment above a shuffled background for each gene 3

region.  Sequences in regions containing high confidence (≥ 0.99) RBFOX2-STAMP edits were significantly 4

enriched for the UGCAUG RBFOX2 binding motif, and the enrichments were correlated with the doxycycline 5

dose and subsequent expression levels of RBFOX2-STAMP (Figure 1H). Importantly, no level of control-STAMP 6

expression at any window size or confidence level derived the (U)GCAUG motif (Figure 1H) and we noted that 7

comparison of all detectible edits from high control- and RBFOX2-STAMP inductions resulted in only a 3.3% 8

overlap in edit sites, demonstrating the sensitivity and specificity of STAMP for determining RBP binding sites. 9

STAMP identifies known RNA targets in multiple RBP backgrounds 1

2

Next we generated two additional HEK293T RBP-STAMP cell lines, one that inducibly expresses 3

APOBEC1 fused to the histone stem-loop binding protein SLBP, and another that expresses a fusion to the 4

stress granule protein TIA1 that binds target mRNA 3’UTRs [3, 33, 34].  SLBP has a very specific set of 5

characterized RNA targets, binding histone mRNAs at 20 nucleotide stem loop regions near the very 3’ end of 6

3’UTRs preceding non-polyadenylated cleavage sites [33].  Comparison of SLBP-STAMP to SLBP eCLIP data 7

[35] showed that SLBP-STAMP edits were reproducibly enriched compared to control-STAMP in close proximity 8

(within 50 nucleotides upstream or downstream) from replicate SLBP eCLIP peaks within the 3’UTR of histone 9

genes, such as H1-2 (Figure 2A) and H4C12 (Figure 2B) adjacent to stem loop regions, as expected.  We 0

calculated e scores for SLBP-STAMP on SLBP eCLIP peaks within histone CDS and 3’UTR regions and saw 1

that the fraction of SLBP eCLIP peaks that contained high e scores increased relative to the fraction of randomly 2

located regions (Figure 2C).  Comparison of either merged or replicate SLBP-STAMP e scores to RBFOX2- 3

STAMP e scores across all 12,149 genes edited by either RBP revealed RBP-specific edit enrichment (RBFOX2 4

eCLIP targets in blue, SLBP histone gene targets in magenta), further demonstrating that STAMP editing 5

reflected the binding specificity of the fused RBP (Figure 2D, Figure S2A). 6

Much like RBFOX2- and SLBP-STAMP, comparison of control- and TIA1-STAMP to TIA1 eCLIP revealed 7

that there was reproducible C-to-U edit enrichment arising from low and high level TIA1-STAMP on a significantly 8

enriched eCLIP 3’UTR peak within the TMCO1 gene (Figure 2E). Transcriptome-wide, the TIA1-STAMP edit 9

fraction was enriched around eCLIP peaks based upon e scores (Figure 2F), and high confidence edits (≥0.999) 0

were able to extract the known eCLIP established U(A)-rich binding motif specific for TIA1 at high doxycycline 1

induction (Figure 2G). As with RBFOX2-STAMP, we saw that the number of TIA1-STAMP edits on target genes 2

increased with doxycycline concentration and were strongly correlated across replicates (Figure S2B), and IDR 3

analysis revealed thousands of reproducible edit clusters that increased in number with increasing induction 4

levels (Figure S2C). These results confirm the versatility of the STAMP approach in specifically and reproducibly 5

detecting the targets and binding sites of multiple RBPs. 6

Ribosome-subunit STAMP (Ribo-STAMP) edits are enriched in highly translated coding sequences and 8

responsive to mTOR inhibition. 9

0

Since ribosomes have extensive association with mRNAs during translation, we reasoned that ribosomal 1

subunits fused to APOBEC1 (Ribo-STAMP) have the potential to edit mRNAs in a manner that reflects ribosome 2

association. We had previously observed that eCLIP of small ribosomal subunit RPS3 featured binding patterns 3

that recapitulated the average profile captured by ribosome profiling [3]. Here, we generated independent 4

HEK293T cell lines expressing APOBEC1 fusions to ribosomal subunits RPS2 and RPS3.  For RPS2-STAMP 5

and RPS3-STAMP we observed that C-to-U edits were enriched relative to control-STAMP on exons of protein- 6

coding genes that are highly translated in HEK293T cells, such as ATP5BP [36], coincident with RPS3 eCLIP 7

signal enrichment over size-matched input control (Figure 3A). In comparison, RPS2-STAMP and RPS3- 8

STAMP signal were minimally detected on non-coding genes such as the lncRNA MALAT1, which is localized 9

to the cytoplasm in mitotic cell lines [37](Figure 3B). We performed replicate RPS2-STAMP and control-STAMP 0

inductions at low and high doxycycline concentrations for 24, 48 and 72 hours and observed high, dose- 1

dependent edit count reproducibility, as well as low overlap (2.8% of all detectable edits) between control-STAMP 2

and RPS2-STAMP edit sites at high induction (Figure S3A, Table S4). 3

To evaluate whether Ribo-STAMP can distinguish genes with varying levels of ribosome occupancy, we 4

compared to published ribo-seq, RiboLace [10] and polysome profiling data [38] obtained from HEK293 cells. 5

We grouped transcripts into ribosome occupancy quartiles as measured by these independent methods and 6

quantified the distribution of e scores from RPS2- and RPS3-STAMP compared to control-STAMP for genes in 7

each quartile.  Absent induction of RPS2-STAMP, e score distributions between RPS2- and control-STAMP were 8

indistinguishable (Figure 3C, left). At low levels of induction, we found that e scores from RPS2-STAMP were 9

significantly higher than control-STAMP, particularly in upper ribosome occupancy quartiles (Figure 3C, middle). 0

These statistically significant differences (Q1, Q2; p < 1e-300, Q3 p = 1e-227, Wilcoxon rank-sum) were 1

accentuated at high induction of RPS2- and control-STAMP conditions (Figure 3C, right, Q1-Q3; p < 1e-300, 2

Wilcoxon rank-sum).  We observed the same effect when comparing RPS2-STAMP to RiboLace (Figure 3D) 3

and polysome profiling (Figure 3E). Because RPS2-STAMP had more consistent signal across CDS regions 4

and higher correlation with independent ribosome foot-printing approaches than RPS3-STAMP (Figure 3F), we 5

proceeded with RPS2-STAMP as the representative Ribo-STAMP fusion for downstream analysis. Meta-coding 6

gene analysis of RPS2-STAMP edits for the top quartile of ribosome occupied genes revealed enrichment of 7

edits within the CDS when compared to control-STAMP background edits and RBFOX2-STAMP edits, which 8

showed the expected 3’UTR profile consistent with eCLIP (Figure 3G). Enrichment of RPS2-STAMP edits within 9

3’UTRs likely indicates ribosome association with these accessible regions following ribosome translation 0

termination by release factors, as we also observed 3’UTR signal from RPS3 eCLIP (Figure 3A). 1

To determine if Ribo-STAMP edits detect translational perturbations, we performed stable high-induction 2

RPS2- and control-STAMP and simultaneously treated cells with the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) 3

pathway inhibitor Torin-1, a selective ATP-competitive inhibitor of mTOR kinase [39].  Pharmacological inhibition 4

of the mTOR pathway globally suppresses translation of mRNAs after initially suppressing translation of genes 5

encoding the translational machinery itself [40].  48-hour Torin-1 treatment resulted in reproducible suppression 6

in RPS2-STAMP edit distributions compared to untreated cells, exemplified by a marked decrease specifically 7

in coding sequence edits on the top quartile of ribosome occupied genes (ribo-seq, Figure 3H). RPS2-STAMP 8

e scores were also significantly reduced upon 48-hour Torin-1 treatment in the highest quartile of ribosome 9

occupied genes as defined by ribo-seq (Q1 p = 3.9 e-98, Wilcoxon rank-sum), RiboLace (Q1 p = 8.4 e-87, 0

Wilcoxon rank-sum) and polysome profiling  (Q1 p = 1.2 e-54, Wilcoxon rank-sum), and all reported Torin-1 1

sensitive TOP genes [40] were contained within these top quartiles (Figure 3H).  We observed no significant 2

differences in e scores for control-STAMP cells upon 48-hour Torin-1 treatment for any matched comparisons 3

Long-read STAMP reveals isoform specific binding profiles. 7

8

Given that STAMP does not require isolation of RBP-protected RNA fragments, unlike commonly 9

performed CLIP assays, we hypothesized that STAMP may enable RNA target detection on full-length mRNA 0

isoforms using long-read sequencing technology.  We performed 72-hour stable high-induction RBFOX2- and 1

control-STAMP and directly sequenced both RNA and cDNA long reads with the Oxford Nanopore sequencing 2

platform [41, 42]. Both of these direct long-read sequencing approaches resulted in enrichment above control of 3

C-to-U edits from RBFOX2-STAMP that overlapped with both eCLIP signal and short read (Illumina) RBFOX2- 4

STAMP signal on the target gene APP 3’UTR (Figure 4A). 5

Long-read high confidence (≥ 0.99) RBFOX2-STAMP edits extracted the known RBFOX2 UGCAUG 6

binding motif using either genomic mapping (hg19; p = 1e-42, hypergeometric distribution) or isoform mapping 7

(cDNA; p = 1e-27, hypergeometric distribution).  Encouraged by the ability to detect RBFOX2 edits on cDNA 8

alignments we wanted to evaluate if there were any isoform-specific binding events. To accomplish this, we 9

counted RBFOX2-STAMP or control-STAMP edits above confidence level 0.99 on the primary and secondary 0

isoforms of 1,631 RBFOX2 eCLIP target genes, and observed differential isoform editing signatures (Figure 1

4B). To illustrate, displayed edits on the UNK (Figure 4C, D) and IDS (Figure S4A, B) genes and observed 2

RBFOX2-STAMP (but not control-STAMP) isoform specific edits, implying isoform-specific binding by RBFOX2 3

to these transcripts. These results demonstrate that STAMP enables isoform-aware long-read detection of RBP- 4

RNA interactions. 5

Detection of RBFOX2-RNA targets at single-cell resolution 7

8

To evaluate whether STAMP can discover RBP-RNA interactions in single cells, we leveraged a 9

commercially available single-cell capture platform. We modified our plasmid vectors to enable capture by the 0

10x Genomics Single Cell 3’ v3 beads and performed 72-hour stable high-induction RBFOX2- and control- 1

STAMP in distinct HEK293T cell-lines followed by standard single-cell (sc)RNA-seq. Using the inserted capture- 2

sequence adjacent to the RBP open-reading frames to identify “capture cells” we identified 854 true RBFOX2- 3

STAMP cells to compare to 5,242 control-STAMP cells. 4

Comparison of bulk and single-cell edit fractions for control- and RBFOX2-STAMP experiments across 5

the top 200 expressed genes (ranked by transcripts per million from bulk RBFOX2-STAMP RNA-seq) revealed 6

nearly identical edit enrichment profiles of RBFOX2 samples above controls and further uncovered a spectrum 7

of editing frequencies across individual cells (Figure 5A).  Both the number of edited genes (Figure S5A) and 8

the summed e score per cell (Figure S5B) were higher in RBFOX2-STAMP cells compared to control-STAMP 9

cells, and single-cell RBFOX2-STAMP edits were detected on 71% of genes that also contained bulk RBFOX2- 0

STAMP edits, with only 7% of single-cell edited genes not detected in bulk (Figure S5C). For normalized edit 1

counts across all expressed gene 3’UTRs (n = 15,832 genes, confidence level ≥ 0.9), bulk and single-cell 2

RBFOX2-STAMP showed strong correlation (Figure 5B, R2 = 0.61, p < 1e-300, two-sided test with R beta 3

distribution). We next ranked individual control- and RBFOX2-STAMP cells by summed e score and visualized 4

edit fractions for the top 10 cells on the RBFOX2 eCLIP target gene UQCRH.  For all 10 selected RBFOX2- 5

Deconvolution of RBP- and cell type-specific RNA binding 2

3

The ability of STAMP to recover RBP-RNA targets in single cells suggests that targets of multiple RBPs 4

could be simultaneously discovered from a single multiplexed experiment. In our RBFOX2-STAMP experiment, 5

we separately performed 72-hour high-induction TIA1-STAMP, prior to mixing equal number of RBFOX2- and 6

TIA1-STAMP cells, followed by scRNA-seq. Cells harboring capture sequences for TIA1- and RBFOX2-STAMP 7

were far better distinguished by UMAP visualization using e scores, than by gene expression (Figure 6A, S6A), 8

congruent with our expectations that the single-cell e score profiles of TIA1- and RBFOX2-STAMP targets were 9

sufficiently distinct. UMAP visualization of e scores further revealed that control-STAMP cells (n = 8,117 cells) 0

were distinct from RBFOX2- and TIA-STAMP “capture cells” (Figure 6B). Using Louvain clustering by e score 1

profiles we thus defined an RBFOX2-cluster (n = 6,003 cells), a TIA1-cluster (n = 1,841 cells) and a 2

“background”-cluster (n = 6,623 cells) for further analysis (Figure S6B). Overlap with control (Figure 6C) and 3

re-clustering in the expression space (Figure S6C) for these defined clusters highlighted the utility of e score- 4

based clustering for defining RBP-specific cell groups. De novo motif analysis of edits from the aggregated cells 5

in the RBFOX2-cluster, but not control, confirmed edit enrichment at RBP-specific binding sites (Figure S6D), 6

and TIA1-and RBFOX2-clusters displayed distinct editing profiles when compared to control-STAMP (Figure 7

6D, Table S5). We ranked cells based on summed e scores to select cells with the most robust editing and found 8

that the top 5 cells for each RBP displayed edit enrichment on the shared RBFOX2- and TIA1-STAMP target 9

NPM1. Individual cell edit enrichments were specific to TIA1-STAMP on the BTF3 target gene, and to RBFOX2- 0

STAMP on the CFL1 target gene (Figure 6E), demonstrating that the targets and binding sites of multiplexed 1

RBP-STAMP fusions can be delineated from edit signatures within single-cell experiments. 2

We next set out to identify cell-type specific RBP targets using single-cell STAMP. We performed STAMP 3

in HEK293T cells and pluripotent stem cell-derived neural progenitor cells (NPCs) [43] by transient transfection 4

with plasmids constitutively expressing either RBFOX2- or control-STAMP fusions, and then mixed equal 5

numbers of HEK293T and NPC cells for each STAMP construct before performing scRNA-seq. 6

UMAP visualization revealed that cells clustered by gene expression into distinct HEK293T and NPC subgroups 7

expressing cell-type specific markers (Figure 6F, Figure S6E, Table S6).  UMAP clustering on e score also 8

resulted in separation of cell types (as determined by gene expression clustering) based on RBFOX2-STAMP 9

edits (Figure 6G, Table S7), and we extracted the RBFOX2 binding motif using edit clusters from 2,178 NPC 0

cells editing 468 target genes, and 3,258 HEK293 cells editing 939 target genes (Figure S6F). Analysis of the 1

top RBFOX2-STAMP differentially edited genes between cell types revealed cell-type specific targets (Figure 2

each cell-type ranked by summed e score illustrated targets that were edited specifically in HEK293 cells such 5

targets and binding sites can be extracted from RBFOX2-STAMP edit signatures by scRNA-seq within a mixture 7

Ribo-STAMP reveals translational landscapes at single-cell resolution. 0

1

To examine whether Ribo-STAMP can quantify ribosome association at the single-cell level, we 2

performed stable 72-hour high-induction control- and RPS2-STAMP and conducted scRNA-seq. UMAP 3

visualization of single-cell, transcriptome-wide e scores revealed that control-STAMP cells overlapped with a 4

subpopulation of RBFOX2-, TIA1- and RPS2-STAMP cells (Figure S7A), highlighting cells that have similar 5

background-level edit patterns. Louvain clustering within UMAP projection space defined four distinct groups of 6

single cells for downstream analysis: (i) RPS2-cluster cells (n = 3,868 cells), (ii) RBFOX2-cluster cells (n = 7,000 7

Discussion 8

We have developed STAMP and its companion computational workflow as a framework that allows 9

antibody-free detection of RBP and ribosome interactomes (Ribo-STAMP) by standard RNA sequencing and 0

quantification of binding-site-specific C-to-U edits directed by RBP- and ribosomal subunit-APOBEC1 fusions, 1

respectively. The recently published DART-seq approach was used to mark m6A RNA modifications genome 2

wide [25], however it was unclear if the method would work for general classes of full-length RBPs and even 3

ribosomes. To distinguish our framework, which showcases unprecedented single-cell resolution binding sites 4

of a broad range of RBPs and ribosome subunits, from DART-seq (a portion of the YTH-domain) and TRIBE 5

(ADAR deaminase domains), we call our framework STAMP (Surveying Targets by Apobec-mediated Profiling). 6

We were able to demonstrate the specificity of STAMP for diverse, full-length RBPs that bind both polyadenylated 7

mRNAs (RBFOX2, TIA1) and non-polyadenylated mRNAs (SLBP). We also demonstrate that ribosomal subunits 8

RPS2 and RPS3 when fused to APOBEC1 enable the measurement of ribosome association that correlates well 9

with metrics such as translation efficiency computed from ribo-seq, RiboLace and polysome profiling experiments 0

which often require separate mRNA-seq data as normalizing denominators. In a single experiment, Ribo-STAMP 1

uses edited and non-edited reads to reflect ribosome-associated and input gene expression values 2

simultaneously. We found that Ribo-STAMP signal was sensitive to mTOR pathway inhibition, showcasing 3


<!-- Page 12 -->


responsiveness to specific translational perturbations. Furthermore, with single-cell Ribo-STAMP we observed 4

that cell populations with gene expression signatures characteristic of the M phase of the mitotic cell cycle were 5

enriched for edits on M phase translated genes. This was consistent with data by standard ribosome profiling in 6

M phase arrested cells [45-47], highlighting the potential of single-cell Ribo-STAMP to simultaneously examine 7

both transcriptional and translational levels of gene expression control.  We envision that these simultaneous 8

readouts will be extremely useful in more complex and heterogeneous cellular or in vivo models to address 9

questions concerning cell identity or disease states. To enable dissemination of our single-cell STAMP 0

technologies, we also developed computational methods that demultiplex multiple RBPs by clustering cells using 1

only edit signatures, which we can validate using 10x feature barcoding technology. 2

STAMP has distinct advantages over TRIBE, as TRIBE generally yields only gene-level target information 3

and not binding sites, with one to two edits on average detectable in any given target [18, 19, 21, 22]. The sparse 4

editing signal by ADAR deaminase domains is due to the preference for ADAR to edit double-stranded RNAs 5

that contain a bulged mismatch [23], an infrequent occurrence on single stranded mRNAs transcriptome-wide 6

[18, 23, 48]. In contrast, APOBEC enzymes access cytosines in single-stranded RNA which constitute ~25%- 7

35% of nucleotides in any given mammalian transcript and produce clusters of edits (between 10 and 1000 edits 8

at target sites). We observe this density of edits with full-length RBPs, but it is apparent even with only the YTH 9

domain of the m6a reader YTHDF2 [25]. In addition, structured RNA is reduced from coding regions by active 0

translation [49], making ribosome interactions that are easily detectable by Ribo-STAMP not feasible with ADAR- 1

fusion approaches. Indeed, the RBP FMR1 fusions to ADAR, which is expected to be very frequent in the coding 2

regions of genes resulted in only 4 confident edits across the ~15kb coding region of the showcased POE gene 3

[18]. The higher likelihood of encountering APOBEC1 cytosine substrates within single-stranded mRNA enables 4

STAMP-mediated discovery of RBP-RNA sites with such high sensitivity and specificity that de novo discovery 5

of conserved binding-site motifs can be extracted from transcripts in even one single cell. 6

Antibody-based methodologies such as CLIP and RIP are staples used to identify RNA binding sites and 7

targets of RBPs. Our STAMP approach offers several advantages. First, with eCLIP-seq as a comparison, we 8

are constrained by the input requirements, frequently needing thousands to millions of cells for a successful 9

eCLIP experiment. Here we demonstrate that STAMP can be used reliably at single-cell resolution to identify 0

RNA targets, binding sites and even extract motifs from a few to a single cell. STAMP enables the combined 1

identification of RBP binding sites and global measurement of gene expression, a long-standing goal for the 2

gene expression, genomics and RNA communities. As a result, even without single cell analyses, STAMP is 3

permissive of ultra-low input material which enables rare cell-types to be collected and analyzed for RBP- 4

interactomes. Second, CLIP requires fragmentation to separate bound and unbound RNA, but that precludes 5

the discovery of isoform-dependent binding sites on mRNAs that may differ by an exon or translated regions. 6

We show here that STAMP allows long-read assessment to distinguish RBP binding on different transcript 7

isoforms. Further, direct RNA sequencing has recently been demonstrated to be RNA-modification sensitive [50], 8

which opens the possibility of using STAMP to detect modification-sensitive RNA-protein interactions. 9

Caveats and considerations 1


<!-- Page 13 -->


Current versions of STAMP have several limitations. In our study, we utilized polyA+ mRNA-sequencing 2

(other than total RNA-seq for SLBP-STAMP) to characterize binding interactions for RBFOX2, TIA1, RPS2 and 3

RPS3. However, aside from their roles mediated by interacting with sites in mRNA, RBFOX2 and TIA1 are also 4

splicing factors with binding sites within intronic regions which are missed by polyA selection of mRNAs. 5

Adaptation of the approach to use nuclear isolation, non-polyA selection with the removal of ribosomal RNA 6

contaminants (as we performed for SLBP), or targeted sequencing of intronic regions are strategies anticipated 7

to recover these binding events. On the other hand, false positive binding sites are also possible when expression 8

levels of STAMP transgenes are supra-physiological, leading to promiscuous RNA interactions. Expression of 9

fusions from a native promoter could help address this concern. Certainly, RBP-STAMP signal that does not 0

overlap with traditional CLIP peaks may indeed be bona fide binding events that CLIP methodologies are not 1

sensitive enough to detect. Unlike RBFOX2, SLBP and TIA1 that have conserved and narrow binding sites, other 2

RBPs may exhibit broad binding patterns across the sequence of the transcripts, such as the ribosomal subunits 3

RPS2 and RPS3. 4

Our current version of Ribo-STAMP yields detectable edits within 12-24 hours. However, we do observe 5

gene expression changes on a subset of genes at high Ribo-STAMP induction after 72 hours, likely due to 6

recoding of transcripts and the possible introduction of nonsense or frameshift mutations. Therefore, it is 7

important to consider the duration of expression of Ribo-STAMP as it may lead to downstream unintended 8

perturbations.  If longer time frames are needed, use of STAMP with the ribosome associated factors, such as 9

translation initiation or release factors, may allow detection of translation responses without long-term coding 0

sequence perturbations.  Alternatively, we can develop more rapid and responsive ribosome directed edits to 1

achieve snapshots of translatome responses on shorter timescales. Extended Ribo-STAMP expression could 2

also explain the somewhat unexpected 3’UTR edit enrichment that we observed, although 3’UTR enrichment of 3

edits appears to be a generalized phenomenon for both TRIBE/HyperTRIBE and DART-seq approaches, likely 4

due to editing modules accessing susceptible 3’UTR sequence elements distal to actual fusion binding sites [18, 5

20, 21, 25]. EIF4E-BP-HyperTRIBE, which sought to use A-to-I editing to mark 5’ ends of translationally 6

repressed transcripts, observed a similar 3’UTR enrichment to Ribo-STAMP, which was potentially explained by 7

5’ and 3’ end association of translation components and mRNA features [20]. In the future, we anticipate that 8

engineering of fusion orientation, altering STAMP expression levels and duration of overexpression window may 9

be useful to obtain editing profiles that are maximally informative for different RBPs. 0

Looking ahead, as STAMP allows isoform-aware and single-cell level interrogation of RNA-protein 1

interactions, we anticipate that focused genomic integrations of editing modules in animal and organoid models 2

will be powerful for in vivo tracing of RNA-protein interaction landscapes in many previously inaccessible 3

contexts.  Previously, cell type-specific CLIP or Ribo-seq from in vivo models has remained a challenge in the 4

field. The STAMP approach, utilizing cell-type specific promoters and gene expression profiles, would overcome 5

these major challenges. Organoid or animal model systems expressing STAMP fusions for RBPs of interest hold 6

the potential to unveil the isoform specific RNA binding and translation landscapes at the organismal level, which 7

would also allow for tissue and cell type-specific profiling in developmental or disease relevant phenotypes. 8

eCLIP 0

TIA1 eCLIP experiments were performed as previously described in a detailed standard operating procedure [2], 1

which is provided as associated documentation with each eCLIP experiment on the ENCODE portal 2

(https://www.encodeproject.org/documents/fa2a3246-6039-46ba-b960- 3

17fe06e7876a/@@download/attachment/CLIP_SOP_v1.0.pdf). In brief, 20 million crosslinked cells were lysed 4

and sonicated, followed by treatment with RNase I (Thermo Fisher) to fragment RNA. Antibodies were pre- 5

coupled to species-specific (anti-rabbit IgG or anti-mouse IgG) Dynabeads (Thermo Fisher), added to lysate, 6


<!-- Page 48 -->


and incubated overnight at 4 °C. Prior to IP washes, 2% of sample was removed to serve as the paired input 7

sample. For IP samples, high- and low-salt washes were performed, after which RNA was dephosphorylated 8

with FastAP (Thermo Fisher) and T4 PNK (NEB) at low pH, and a 3′ RNA adaptor was ligated with T4 RNA 9

ligase (NEB). Ten per cent of IP and input samples were run on an analytical PAGE Bis-Tris protein gel, 0

transferred to PVDF membrane, blocked in 5% dry milk in TBST, incubated with the same primary antibody used 1

for IP (typically at 1:4,000 dilution), washed, incubated with secondary HRP-conjugated species-specific TrueBlot 2

antibody (Rockland), and visualized with standard enhanced chemiluminescence imaging to validate successful 3

IP. Ninety per cent of IP and input samples were run on an analytical PAGE Bis-Tris protein gel and transferred 4

to nitrocellulose membranes, after which the region from the protein size to 75 kDa above protein size was 5

excised from the membrane, treated with proteinase K (NEB) to release RNA, and concentrated by column 6

purification (Zymo). Input samples were then dephosphorylated with FastAP (Thermo Fisher) and T4 PNK (NEB) 7

at low pH, and a 3′ RNA adaptor was ligated with T4 RNA ligase (NEB) to synchronize with IP samples. Reverse 8

transcription was then performed with AffinityScript (Agilent), followed by ExoSAP-IT (Affymetrix) treatment to 9

remove unincorporated primer. RNA was then degraded by alkaline hydrolysis, and a 3′ DNA adaptor was ligated 0

with T4 RNA ligase (NEB). qPCR was then used to determine the required amplification, followed by PCR with 1

Q5 (NEB) and gel electrophoresis to size-select the final library. Libraries were sequenced on the HiSeq 2000, 2

2500, or 4000 platform (Illumina). Each ENCODE eCLIP experiment consisted of IP from two independent 3

biosamples, along with one paired size-matched input (sampled from one of the two IP lysates before IP washes). 4

Reproducible eCLIP peaks were called using the latest release of the core pipeline 5

(https://github.com/yeolab/eclip), followed by a peak merging sub-workflow to identify reproducible peaks 6

(https://github.com/YeoLab/merge_peaks). 7

Bulk RNAseq was sequenced single-end 100nt and trimmed using cutadapt (v1.14.0). Trimmed reads were 0

did not map to repeats were then mapped to the hg19 assembly with STAR, sorted with samtools (v1.5) and 2

quantified against Gencode (v19) annotations using Subread featureCounts (v1.6.3). Genes with zero counts 3

summed across all samples were removed prior to performing differential expression analysis using DESeq2 4

(v1.26.0) [3]. 5
